program: Travel English -- Europe Without a Translator
hub_subtitle: Travel English for the airport, the check-in counter, the hotel and passport control — so that Europe needs no translator

lesson.menu_title: Rosângela Is Ready -- Twenty Lessons, and the Road Behind
lesson.menu_desc: The last lesson of the program. It opens with the five sentences from the Lesson 1 survival card — word for word, everything she could say at a departure gate twenty lessons ago — and asks her to say the same things the way she says them today. The new tool is the one that measures a road: for for a period, since for the moment it started, and the question every traveler asks, How long have you been here? New words for looking back and looking ahead: to come a long way, progress, a milestone, to rely on, to manage, proud of, to look back, step by step, to keep it up, a goal -- 39 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 20 -- Rosângela Is Ready
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Rosângela | Lesson 20 -- Rosângela Is Ready
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect with for and since for duration (How long have you been here? / I've been here since Monday / for two weeks)

listenings.text: My name is Andrew, and I am the night manager of a small hotel in Lisbon. I have stood behind the same front desk since two thousand and three, so that is twenty-two years of watching people arrive at eleven at night with a suitcase and a face. And I am going to tell you something I have never said to a guest. I can tell in about ten seconds which of them are traveling on their own. It has nothing to do with who is alone. Couples arrive, families arrive, groups of six arrive. What I watch is where the eyes go when I start speaking. Some guests look at me. Some guests look at the person beside them, and wait. And when that happens, I end up giving the information to the wrong pair of ears, because the person who is listening is not the person who is going to walk out of that door tomorrow morning and look for the tram. The trip belongs to whoever is listening. That is not always the person who paid for the room. Now, the part that took me twenty years to understand. Guests come back. Not many, but some, three years later, five years later, and here is what I notice about their English. It is the same. The same small mistakes, the same missing words, the same slow start. Nothing improved, and it made no difference at all. Because the second time, they ask me the question themselves, and they stay for the answer, and they ask a second one. That is the whole change. Not better grammar. A different pair of eyes.

It is Teresa again. I am the one who rehearsed her whole journey out loud in her kitchen, to nobody, two weeks before her first trip alone. Well, I went. And I have been home for two weeks now, and I want to tell you what really happened, because it is not what I expected. I used almost none of the sentences I rehearsed. Almost none of them. The airport did not go the way I had practiced, the shuttle was in a different place, the woman at passport control asked me something about my return ticket that I had never thought about. And I want to say clearly that this was not a problem, because it took me a few days to understand why. The rehearsal was never a script. The rehearsal was practice at opening my mouth. On the second day, the hotel had no record of my booking. None. I had never practiced that sentence, not once, and I said it badly, in the wrong order, with the wrong verb, twice. And the woman at the desk understood me anyway and found the reservation under my first name. Twenty minutes, and it was over, and I went upstairs, and I sat on the bed and I laughed. So here is what I do now. I have already booked the next trip, for the spring. And I still stand in my kitchen for twenty minutes a day and speak English to nobody, and my daughter still thinks I have lost my mind. Keep it up after the lessons stop. That is the only thing I have to say. The lessons end. The traveler does not.

structure.title: Three cards, and every answer about time
cards: Use for when you can count the time: for ten months, for two weeks, for forty years, for a few days. "I've studied English for ten months." "We've been married for forty years." The test: could you measure it with a clock or a calendar page? Then it is for.

Use since when you can point at the moment it started: since Monday, since 2019, since March, since my first trip, since I retired. "We've been here since Monday." "I haven't needed a translator since March." The test: could you circle it on a calendar? Then it is since.

This is the question you will hear at every breakfast table in Europe: "How long have you been in Portugal?" Both answers work: "For twelve days" or "Since the second of May". And it is never "How long are you here" — the duration question always carries have or has.

reading.rtitle: A Letter From One Year Ahead
paras: I am Marina, I am sixty-four, and I live in Curitiba. I finished my twenty lessons in March last year, so I have been on my own for more than a year now, and somebody asked me to write this for the people who are sitting in their last lesson tonight. So here is the first honest thing, before anything else. In my first month without lessons I did nothing. Not one word, not one video, not one minute. And it frightened me, because I could feel how fast it went quiet in my head. This letter is not about how wonderful the course was. It is about the month after.

Three things saved it, and all three are small. First: I had already booked the next trip. That was luck and not planning, but it turned out to be everything, because a date on the calendar changes what you do on a Tuesday night. Book the next trip before the last lesson. Second: twenty minutes a day, out loud, in the kitchen, with nobody listening. Not studying — talking. Third, and this is the hard one: I say yes to every conversation. The woman at the airport, the man in the next seat, the receptionist who asks how long I have been in the city. I used to smile and look at my telephone. Now I answer, and then I ask something back.

And now the thing nobody tells you. I never became fluent. My grammar today is more or less the grammar I had on my last day, and I still make the same three mistakes I made in that lesson. It has not mattered once. What changed is not inside the sentences: it is that I start them. I have not needed anybody to speak for me since that March — not at a counter, not on the telephone, and not in a hospital in Porto at two in the morning, which is a story for another letter. You are not finishing tonight. You are being handed the thing back. Book the trip. Twenty minutes. Say yes.
reading.source: Marina, 64 — Curitiba, one year after her last lesson

gist.prompt: What is the letter really about?
choices: The cities Marina visited during her year of traveling.
What actually happens after the last lesson, and the three small things that keep the English alive.
Why English courses do not work for people over sixty.

items: Marina finished her English lessons more than a year before writing this letter.
She finished in March of last year and says she has been on her own for more than a year now.
In her first month without lessons, Marina practiced more than she did during the course.
The opposite: she did nothing at all for a month, and it frightened her to feel how fast it went quiet in her head.
The first of Marina's three rules is to book the next trip before the last lesson.
She says booking the trip was luck rather than planning, but that a date on the calendar changes what you do on a Tuesday night.
Marina says the big change after the course was that her grammar got much better.
She says her grammar is more or less the same and she still makes the same three mistakes. What changed is that she starts the conversations instead of waiting.
Marina became fluent during her year on her own.
She says clearly that she never became fluent, and that it has not mattered once: she stopped needing anybody to speak for her, which is a different thing.

items.situation: You are at the breakfast table in Lisbon. Another guest asks: "How long have you been here?" You arrived on Monday and today is Friday.
tips: Since + the day it started: "We've been here since Monday."
Or for + the period: "For four days."
Then give it back: "And you? How long have you been in the city?"

items.situation: A woman on the plane says your English is very good and asks whether you have always spoken it.
tips: Be honest and do not apologize: "No, ten months."
Add the shape of it: "Step by step. I've come a long way."
You can finish with the goal: "Next year, three weeks on my own."

items.situation: At the front desk, the receptionist asks how long you are staying and whether this is your first time in the country.
tips: Duration of the stay: "Four nights, until Sunday."
And the history: "We've been coming to Portugal since 2019."
Add one honest detail: "But this is our first time in this neighborhood."

items.situation: Somebody asks who usually deals with the hotels and the counters when you travel.
tips: The before: "For years I relied on my son."
The now: "But I've done it myself since March."
One example makes it real: "I booked this hotel by email, in English."

items.situation: A traveler asks what has changed for you since your first trip to Europe.
tips: Start with the measurement: "Since 2019 we've been four times."
Then the real answer: "The first time I didn't speak. Now I do all the talking."
Name it: "That was the milestone for me."

items.situation: The person next to you at the gate asks what you are going to do next, now that your course has ended.
tips: Say the habit: "Twenty minutes a day, out loud."
Say the goal: "Three weeks in Portugal next May."
And the reason: "If I keep it up, the trip is easy."
